title: Overview
text: Overview Why simulation? It lets us try an action in a modeled world, calculate what happens, and repeat the experiment with different conditions. This free online book follows one familiar task: opening a drawer. We begin with how AI models understand instructions, then build the 3D object and describe how it moves. Simple explanations, illustrations, and moving examples connect these ideas. Text-only LLM → VLM → VLA — from language to images and robot actions. 3D generation — creating objects and choosing how to represent them. Articulated objects — parts, joints, URDF files, and simulated motion.

title: 1. Text-only LLM → VLM → VLA
text: 1. Text-only LLM → VLM → VLA Suppose we ask a robot to open a drawer. It needs to understand the request, find the handle, and move its arm. These three kinds of model help explain those different abilities. “Open the drawer.” How do words turn into movement?

title: Text-only LLM: work with language
text: 1.1 Text-only LLM: work with language A text-only large language model (LLM) takes text and generates text. It cannot inspect an image directly; you need to describe it in words. It can explain a task or suggest steps to follow. Llama 2 is one example. We ask: “How do you open a drawer?” A possible answer: “Hold the handle and pull outward.” That is a useful instruction, but this text-only exchange does not tell the robot where the handle is in front of it.

title: VLM: connect images and words
text: 1.2 VLM: connect images and words A vision-language model (VLM) can use an image together with text. It can answer questions about what it sees. For example, LLaVA connects an image encoder to a language model. We provide: the cabinet picture and “Which handle belongs to the drawer?” A possible answer: “The handle on the blue part at the top.” Now the answer is tied to this cabinet. The robot still needs commands that move its arm and gripper.

title: VLA: produce robot actions
text: 1.3 VLA: produce robot actions A vision-language-action model (VLA) uses visual information and an instruction to produce robot actions. Depending on the model, it may also use information about the robot’s current position. The output can be numbers telling the gripper where to move and whether to open or close. A separate robot controller carries out those commands. The next camera image shows what actually happened. Opening a drawer, step by step In this example, the gripper is already holding the handle. The diagram illustrates one possible action, not a recorded prediction from a trained model. 1 Camera image + instruction Drawer: 0 cm open Gripper: holding the handle Instruction “Open the drawer.” The image shows the current situation. The words give the task. 2 Inside the VLA Image encoder + adapter Turn the image into numerical features the main model can use. Vision-language backbone Combine those features with the instruction “Open the drawer.” Action output Produce action values. Here, a possible result is an outward movement with the gripper kept closed. 3 A possible command Move outward +0.10 m Gripper Keep closed In words: “Move the gripper 10 cm outward while holding the handle.” These are two readable fields for this one-direction example. A real robot’s command format can include more movement values. 4 Controller → movement → new image The controller tries to execute the command. If the drawer slides freely and the grip holds, the drawer can follow the gripper outward. Possible result: 10 cm open If the drawer is locked, it stays at 0 cm instead. The next camera image shows the actual result, so the next prediction can use that new information. ↺ The new camera image goes back to step 1. The model can then choose another action. What does “predict an action” mean? A VLA is trained using examples that pair observations and instructions with robot actions. It learns patterns in those examples. When given a new image and instruction, it uses what it learned to produce the next action values. For the same instruction, “Open the drawer,” different views can call for different commands: What the image shows Example next command The open gripper is positioned around the handle. Move 0 cm ; close the gripper to grasp it. The gripper is already holding the handle. Move 10 cm outward ; keep closed . These are illustrative commands. Here, “predict” means propose the next action The structure is simplified from OpenVLA , whose predicted outputs are decoded into numerical robot commands. Other VLAs can organize their action outputs differently.

title: What happens after the robot tries to pull?
text: 1.4 What happens after the robot tries to pull? Suppose the gripper is holding the handle. The VLA outputs a command: “Move the gripper 10 cm outward.” This is a requested movement. It does not guarantee that the drawer opens by 10 cm. A freely sliding drawer may follow the gripper. A locked drawer stays shut. A heavy drawer or one with high friction may require more force than the controller can supply. The result depends on the robot, its controller, and the object. A real robot finds out by interacting with the real cabinet. In simulation, we build a model of that interaction and calculate what happens. The VLA requests an action. For example, move the gripper outward while keeping it closed. The controller tries to make that movement. It turns the request into control inputs for the simulated robot. The simulation calculates the response. A physics engine computes how the robot and drawer move under the modeled forces, contacts, and joint limits. A renderer makes the next camera image. The VLA receives this updated view and can choose another action. We can reset the same scene and repeat the task, then change just the drawer’s mass or friction to compare the results. This helps us test a robot’s behavior without rebuilding a physical experiment each time. Simulated experience can also be used for training; its usefulness depends on how well the simulated conditions represent the intended task. What do we need to build that cabinet? A 3D shape The cabinet, drawer, and handle need geometry. This gives us something to render and helps define where contact can happen. Parts and joints The drawer must be a separate moving part, connected so it can slide but cannot move freely in every direction. Physical properties Mass, friction, and contact settings help determine how the object responds to a force. The diagram above illustrates the command-and-feedback loop. Later, we will calculate the drawer’s movement from forces. That is the path through the next two sections: 3D generation explains the object’s shape; Articulated objects adds its moving parts and joints, then forces and simulated motion .

title: 2.1 From an image to a usable 3D object
text: 2.1 From an image to a usable 3D object A robot sees a cabinet in an image. How do we turn that image into something it can open in simulation? We need to recover a shape, decide how to represent it, and give its parts rules for movement.

title: From an image to a usable 3D object
text: A photograph tells us which colors appeared from one camera position. It does not directly give the cabinet’s depth, the shape of its back, or the space inside its drawer. Many different 3D objects could produce a similar front view. Reconstruction tries to recover the particular object or scene in the observations. Photos from several viewpoints help reveal depth and hidden surfaces. Generation uses patterns learned from other objects to create a plausible asset from a prompt or image. With one image, those learned patterns can help fill in unseen regions, but a plausible interior is not necessarily the real interior. Images or text → 3D shape → Movable parts → Physical model These are different levels of information. A beautiful cabinet may still be one fused shape. Separate drawer and body shapes may still have no rule saying that the drawer slides. Even a sliding drawer needs physical properties before we can calculate what a pull will do. This progression—from whole shapes, to parts, to parts with motion—is also the organizing idea in SPARK’s related work . We will first understand the shape and appearance, then connect them to simulation. The full path: a picture, a 3D model, and a new picture Suppose we start with a picture of a cabinet and want to see its other side. We first need a 3D version of the cabinet. We can then put a virtual camera beside it and make a new picture. Input images What the original camera saw. Reconstruct or generate A method estimates a 3D object or scene. Store the 3D result For example, a mesh, 3D Gaussians, or a learned field. Render from a camera Calculate what is visible from a chosen viewpoint. A new 2D image The same 3D result, seen from that viewpoint. Three examples of this path TRELLIS Input: one image. Create: a pretrained generator proposes the object’s 3D form. Save the 3D scene: a mesh or 3D Gaussians, among its supported outputs. Render a 2D image: draw the mesh surfaces, or project and blend the Gaussians. Original 3DGS Input: photographs of a scene from several views, with estimated cameras. Create: adjust Gaussians until their images match those photos. Save the 3D scene: positions, shapes, opacity, and appearance of the Gaussians. Render a 2D image: project and blend them into an image. Original NeRF Input: photographs of a scene from several views, with known camera poses. Create: train a network until its images match those photos. Save the 3D scene: the trained network’s weights. Render a 2D image: query the network along lines of sight and combine its answers. These are alternative routes. TRELLIS can infer unseen sides from its prior training; the original NeRF and 3DGS methods fit one observed scene. A convincing new view does not by itself prove that the hidden geometry is correct. Sources: TRELLIS , 3DGS , and NeRF . How rendering helps us build the 3D model Building a 3D model and rendering an image are opposite directions, but they work together. If we have a candidate 3D cabinet, we can draw it from the same viewpoint as an input photo. Comparing the two images tells us how well the candidate explains what the camera saw. 2D → 3D: estimate Use photographs to construct or adjust a 3D representation. 3D → 2D: render Make a picture from a known camera view. During fitting, compare it with the photograph to check the current estimate. For example, if the rendered handle appears too far left, its 3D position may need to change. Other camera views help distinguish a sideways error from a depth error. Repeating this process is one way to learn a scene from images. The original NeRF and 3DGS methods take photographs of one particular cabinet . They repeatedly adjust their 3D version of that cabinet until its rendered views resemble those photographs. An image-to-3D system such as TRELLIS has already been trained using many different objects . When we give it a new cabinet photo, it uses what it learned to propose a 3D cabinet, including surfaces hidden in that photo. This prior training is what “pretrained” means. For example, TRELLIS can produce a mesh of the cabinet : its shape stored as connected surface patches. It can also produce 3D Gaussians : soft blobs positioned in 3D, which a renderer blends into images. TRELLIS names the system that creates the model; “mesh” or “3D Gaussians” describes the kind of data it produces. We will look at how each works below. One image, two kinds of 3D output Here is a toolbox example published by the TRELLIS authors. The input is one image; the other two pictures show views of the generated 3D outputs. The output pictures use different display modes. The mesh picture shows the surface shape without the wood and metal textures. The Gaussian picture includes the generated appearance. This difference in presentation can make the Gaussian result look more finished. Input image A single 2D picture. Mesh · shape view The surfaces, with the wood and metal appearance omitted. Gaussians · appearance view The generated colors, blended into an image. A mesh can also show wood grain and shiny metal. Its surfaces can carry textures and materials. In fact, the TRELLIS authors also export meshes with appearance transferred from the Gaussians. These pictures therefore do not establish that one representation produces better-looking images. TRELLIS explains its display modes and textured mesh exports . Images: TRELLIS authors’ image-to-3D gallery . Their input image was generated with DALL·E 3. The two output views are frames from the same published example. Why would we choose a mesh? Suppose we want a robot to grasp the toolbox handle. We need to locate the handle’s surface and the gap behind it, edit the shape if necessary, and prepare shapes for contact. A mesh gives us explicit surface patches to work with. We can also organize its geometry into parts before adding joints and physical properties. If our immediate goal is to reproduce the look of a photographed scene from new viewpoints, 3DGS is designed for that rendering task. Its colored blobs can capture appearance without first building a connected surface. The choice depends on what we want to do with the result; surface geometry and Gaussian appearance can also be used together. Original 3DGS project .

title: 2.2 Meshes: surfaces and useful detail
text: 2.2 Meshes: surfaces and useful detail

title: Meshes: surfaces and useful detail
text: A mesh describes surface shape using connected patches . For a drawer, these can describe the outside, the inner walls, and the bottom. The empty space inside the drawer stays empty: a surface mesh does not mean the whole object is filled with material. A point cloud records sampled positions in 3D. A mesh also records how positions connect to form surfaces. The positions are called vertices, their connections are edges, and the surface patches are faces. Moving the positions changes the shape; changing their connections changes how the surface is assembled. Point cloud Useful for recording measurements. Gaps may mean an area was never observed, rather than a real hole. Triangle mesh Explicit surface patches. Triangles are always planar, which makes them convenient for rendering and geometric calculations. Quad mesh Four-sided patches can form regular rows useful for editing and subdivision. They can be triangulated for rendering. Building a mesh from measured points is called surface reconstruction . It must infer which samples belong together; blindly filling every gap could seal the opening around a drawer. Open3D’s examples show several ways to estimate these surfaces. What is Blender used for? Blender is free software for making and editing 3D content. We could open a generated cabinet in Blender, rotate it to inspect the back, build a missing handle, add a wood texture, position lights and a camera, and render an image. It is a working environment for these tasks; a mesh is one kind of data we can edit inside it. The material guide explains how to control the appearance of those surfaces.

title: 2.3 How a 3D model produces a 2D image
text: 2.3 How a 3D model produces a 2D image

title: How a 3D model produces a 2D image
text: A mesh supplies the surfaces of objects in a scene . A scene also specifies where those objects are placed, where the camera looks, and how surfaces are colored and lit. The renderer uses that information to calculate an image. A texture is often an image placed on a surface, like a printed pattern. A material controls how the surface responds to light—for example, whether a handle looks like dull plastic or shiny metal. Which tool makes these pictures? A renderer is the software that calculates the picture. We give it a 3D scene and a virtual camera: where the camera is, which way it looks, and how wide its view is. The software calculates the pixels and saves the result as an image. Think of photographing a cabinet from the left, front, and right. In rendering, we place a virtual camera at those three positions. We keep the same 3D cabinet and calculate a new picture from each position. What we have Example tool What we do A mesh Blender , using a renderer such as Eevee or Cycles. Load the model, set its appearance, place lights and a camera, then render and save an image. 3D Gaussians A Gaussian renderer, such as gsplat . Load the blobs and choose a camera. The renderer projects the blobs and blends their colors into the image. For this book’s Gaussian cabinet videos, we wrote a small renderer in Python. It calculates the projected marks and their color mixtures. The left, front, and right pictures all come from the same cabinet data. Rendering many frames while moving the camera, then joining those frames into a video, gives the moving-camera example in Section 2.4 . A screenshot can record a picture already displayed by a viewer. Here, the renderer saves its calculated images directly. Stored surfaces The mesh gives the cabinet its shape and depth. One camera view The surfaces become colored areas in an image. The construction edges need not be visible. One common mesh-rendering process is rasterization : Project the triangles. Use the camera’s position, viewing direction, and lens to map their 3D corners to 2D image positions. With a perspective camera, a farther object generally appears smaller. Find what each pixel sees. Work out which projected triangles cover it. For opaque surfaces, keep the nearest visible surface; a closed door hides what is behind it. Calculate the color. Use the visible surface’s material, texture, direction, and lighting. Repeat across the image. Imagine walking around a real cabinet: the cabinet stays still, but you see a different side. A virtual camera works similarly. Keep the 3D cabinet in place, move the camera from the front to the side, and render again. The new image shows the surfaces visible from the side. We do not need to rebuild the mesh for that camera movement. This is what the mesh contributes: the cabinet’s surfaces in 3D . The camera chooses the view, and the renderer calculates the picture. More on rendering . We can also make new views using other kinds of stored 3D information. A mesh stores connected surface patches. 3DGS stores many colored, soft 3D blobs ; its renderer blends their projected colors. NeRF stores a trained network ; its renderer asks the network about locations along each line of sight. All three can produce a 2D picture from a chosen camera. Next, we will look at Gaussian rendering in detail.

title: 2.4 3D Gaussian Splatting: build a scene, then render new views
text: 2.4 3D Gaussian Splatting: build a scene, then render new views

title: 3D Gaussian Splatting: build a scene, then render new views
text: Imagine taking photographs while walking around a cabinet. The original 3DGS method uses views like these to build a representation that we can look at from other camera positions. Rendering helps both while building that representation and after it is ready. Build from the photographs Render a trial set of Gaussians, compare its images with the photographs, and adjust the Gaussians to reduce the differences. Explore the finished result Keep the learned Gaussians and move the virtual camera. Render a new view without needing a matching photograph to compare against. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) stores many soft 3D blobs. Each has a position, size, orientation, opacity, and appearance. Imagine one small blue patch on the drawer front. A blob can be wide across that patch but thin from front to back . In the rendered picture, its blue color is strongest at the center and gradually fades toward the edges, like a soft spray-painted spot. Many overlapping spots can form the picture of the whole drawer. How do the 3D blobs become an image? To render a view, the original method projects those blobs into soft 2D ellipses, orders overlapping contributions by depth, and blends their colors. “Splatting” refers to placing these projected marks onto the image. Original 3DGS project . Watch the 3D setup become a 2D view The image plane is a flat rectangle where we draw the camera’s picture. In this diagram it sits in front of the camera. Seen from its edge, that rectangle looks like a line; the image still has width and height. Open the projection video . 0:00 · The setup 0:06 · Project the blobs 0:16 · Look from the edge 0:26 · Face the image 0:36 · Move the camera First, we rotate our view of the diagram to see the image plane from the side and front. In the last part, the camera itself moves while the two 3D blobs stay in place. The picture on the right shows exactly what that camera renders. The outlined shapes help us see the blobs in 3D. Their rendered marks have soft edges because a Gaussian fades outward. Download the video In the last part, watch the gold mark move behind the blue one, then separate again. The 3D blobs have not moved: the camera now sees them along different lines of sight. Their marks are calculated again for each new camera position. This is how the same 3D scene can produce different 2D pictures. For implementation details, see how gsplat uses the camera and Gaussian shapes to calculate these images . Now try a whole cabinet The same idea works with many blobs. Here, blue blobs form the drawer, gold blobs form the door, and teal blobs form the cabinet body. First we enlarge one drawer blob; then we follow the cabinet’s colors onto the image plane and move the camera. Open the cabinet video . 0:00 · The cabinet 0:10 · One blob, enlarged 0:24 · Project onto the image 0:38 · Move the camera 0:56 · Compare three views The outlined shapes make the individual blobs visible. The camera picture blends their soft marks together. The cabinet stays still throughout; only the camera moves. This is a deliberately simple teaching model we built, not a reconstruction trained from photographs. Download the cabinet video What does changing opacity actually change? Several blobs can cover the same spot in the camera’s picture. We need one final color at that spot. Opacity decides how strongly the front blob contributes and how much of the color behind it can still show through. In the cabinet video, overlapping blue marks combine to form the drawer’s picture. Opacity is part of that blending step. It does not add paint or a texture to a mesh. Try a blue mark in front of a gold mark. Move the slider and watch how much gold remains visible. The gold stays at 80% opacity; only the blue changes. Two soft projected ellipses overlap at a marked pixel, with the blue contribution in front of the gold One pixel The marked pixel receives color from both overlapping blobs. Blue opacity at the marked pixel 25% Try 25% Try 85% The resulting pixel 25% blue + 60% gold + 15% white background. Blue uses 25% of the pixel’s weight. Gold gets 80% of the remaining 75%: 60%. The background gets the last 15%. Low blue opacity: more gold shows through. High blue opacity: the picture becomes mostly blue at the marked spot. Neither blob has moved; we have changed how their colors combine. The calculation follows one pixel. Across the whole picture, each mark fades toward its edges, and many marks overlap to make the cabinet’s surfaces look continuous. The 3DGS paper gives the projection and blending equations. Change opacity on the whole cabinet Now change the opacity of every blob in the cabinet . The camera, colors, positions, and sizes stay the same. Compare your setting on the right with the fixed picture on the left. 95% per blob · reference 5% per blob · your setting Opacity of each cabinet blob 5% Try 5% Try 25% Try 95% At 5%, the faint marks let more of the rear surfaces and white background show through. Many blobs overlap. Their colors build up, so 25% per blob does not mean that the whole cabinet is only 25% opaque. At 0%, none of the blobs contributes color and only the white background remains. How are the blobs found from photographs? Imagine walking around this cabinet and photographing it. Keep the drawer and door still: the photographs should describe the same scene from different views . This is a teaching diagram. Rendered cabinet views stand in for photographs; the stages below illustrate the process, rather than showing a recorded training run. 1. Find the same detail in different photographs View 1 View 2 View 3 A marks the same cabinet corner in all three views. Software matches recognizable details across photos. From many such matches, it estimates where the cameras were and where the details sit in 3D. Locate one point. Each view gives a line of sight toward A. Combining views estimates its depth. Repeat for many details. The result is sparse: scattered points, with gaps between them. This camera-and-point estimation is called Structure from Motion (SfM) . COLMAP is one tool for it. A plain, featureless panel can provide few reliable matches; we do not yet have a complete cabinet surface. 2. Put an initial blob at each 3D point Initial 3D blobs Points now have size, color, and opacity. Their rendered 2D image The drawer and handle look blurry. Reference view The image we want to match. Compare from the same camera position. Otherwise, a difference could simply come from looking at the cabinet from a different angle. 3. Use the image differences to update the blobs Render 3D blobs → 2D image → Compare Rendered image ↔ photo → Update Change the 3D blobs ↶ Render again, compare again, update again. The comparison gives an error: how different are the images? The fitting process uses that error to adjust the blobs. For example, several smaller blobs can describe the handle more precisely than one large, blurry blob. Adjust Change position, size, orientation, color, or opacity. Add detail Clone a blob, or split a large one into smaller ones. Remove Discard blobs with very low opacity. These changes happen in 3D , so they affect several camera views. The original 3DGS method alternates parameter updates with adding and removing blobs. 4. Keep checking the other views, too A closer match Many overlapping blobs form a clearer cabinet image. A new camera view Render the same 3D blobs from another position. Fitting repeats across the photographs so that one set of 3D blobs explains many views . We save those blobs and can then render new views. This is the purpose of the 3DGS representation ; it does not automatically add a drawer joint or the cabinet’s mass.

title: 3.1 What is an articulated object?
text: 3.1 What is an articulated object? An articulated object is made of parts that can move relative to one another. A drawer slides. A door swings. The cabinet holds them together. In the previous section, we described the cabinet’s shape. Now we add the parts and connections that let it move. We will first choose the drawer’s position ourselves, then later calculate its motion from a pulling force. Watch the cabinet animation. Body Stays fixed in this example. Drawer Slides in and out along a straight line. Door Rotates around its hinge.

title: Links and joints
text: 3.1.1 Links and joints We describe this cabinet using two building blocks: links and joints . Link A rigid part: its shape stays the same as it moves. The body, drawer, and door are three links. Joint A connection that defines how two links can move relative to each other. The door’s hinge connects the door to the body and lets it rotate. A handle fixed to the door moves together with the door, so it can be included in the same link. A handle that turns independently needs its own link and joint.

title: How joints let parts move
text: 3.1.2 How joints let parts move The drawer and door move in different ways. Move the sliders to try each joint. Sliding Prismatic joint Drawer opening 20 cm 0 cm 50 cm The direction stays the same. Only the distance changes. Rotating Revolute joint Door opening 35° 0° 90° The hinge stays in place. Only the angle changes. The allowed range is the joint’s motion limit . Here, the drawer opens from 0 to 50 cm, and the door from 0° to 90°. These are illustrative limits; another cabinet may allow different motion.

title: Degrees of freedom
text: 3.1.3 Degrees of freedom One articulated object can have several degrees of freedom. This cabinet is one object, but it has two movable joints: one for the drawer and one for the door. A degree of freedom (DOF) is an independent motion you can control. With the cabinet body held fixed: Part Independent control DOF Drawer How far it slides 1 Door How far it rotates 1 Whole cabinet Drawer and door move independently 2 You can leave the door still and move the drawer. You can also leave the drawer still and move the door. So describing the whole cabinet’s pose takes two numbers : the drawer’s opening distance and the door’s opening angle. Here, each joint has 1 DOF; the whole cabinet has 2 DOF. Opening the drawer farther changes its position, but it still has the same one degree of freedom.

title: Kinematic trees
text: 3.1.4 Kinematic trees A kinematic tree records which parts are connected. Each node is a link; each connecting line is a joint. The body is the root : the starting link of this tree. It is the parent of the drawer and door; they are its children . The tree describes connections, not the parts’ positions on the page. In the example below, we add a turning latch to the drawer. The latch can turn independently, adding one more degree of freedom: this version has 3 DOF . Select a part in the tree, then play its motion. The object Its connections hinge slide turn Body Door Drawer Latch Drawer. Slides relative to the body. The latch comes along because it is attached to the drawer. Play drawer motion Motion position Reset A moving part carries its children The drawer is the latch’s parent in this tree. When the drawer slides, the latch travels with it. The latch can also turn relative to the drawer. The door is on a different branch, so moving the drawer does not move the door. Not every articulated object forms a tree. Some mechanisms contain closed loops. This example focuses on a tree, where each link other than the root has one parent.

title: Further reading
text: Further reading To compare the motion and connections of a reconstructed object with a reference, continue to the ArticulateArena documentation ↗ .

title: 3.2 Frames, orientation & URDF
text: 3.2 Frames, orientation & URDF A model needs more than its shape. We also need to know which way it faces, where its joints are, and what each position is measured from.

title: The base and the world
text: 3.2.1 The base and the world A coordinate frame is a reference point with three directions: X, Y, and Z. Its reference point is the origin . World frame The scene’s reference. It lets us place the whole cabinet in a room. Base frame The object’s reference, attached to its root link. Here we use the cabinet body as the base. Move the whole cabinet: its base frame moves with it. The room’s world frame stays in place. The base is not necessarily the object’s bottom or its geometric center. Choosing a base also does not lock the object in place. Holding it fixed is a separate choice in the simulator.

title: Which way is up? Which way is front?
text: 3.2.2 Which way is up? Which way is front? For this chapter’s diagrams, we choose +Z up, +X front, and +Y left in the object’s base frame. “Left” is the object’s own left when facing forward. Other models may use different axes for up and front. First find the object’s usual upright pose. Then use its function to choose the front. Left–right symmetry can suggest an orientation, but it does not always distinguish front from back. Cabinet The side you open is the front. An outward drawer motion is a useful clue. Eyeglasses Use how they are worn: here, front points away from the wearer, through the lenses. The arms extend toward the back. Unmarked box Shape alone may not reveal a unique front. Choose a convention and record it.

title: From a tree to a URDF file
text: 3.2.3 From a tree to a URDF file URDF stands for Unified Robot Description Format. It is a text file that records links and joints, along with their geometry and other properties. Despite its name, it can describe a cabinet too. A joint names its parent and child links. Its type gives the motion rule, axis gives the motion direction in the joint frame, and limit gives the allowed range. Its origin places the joint frame relative to the parent. Before placing the drawer, let’s look at how its shape is stored.

title: What is a mesh?
text: 3.2.4 What is a mesh? A mesh describes a 3D shape using points and flat faces. For the drawer’s orange side panel, those points are its corners. The faces join the points to form its surface. The whole drawer Its sides, bottom, front, and handle move together as one link. One side panel This is one of the drawer’s shapes. The panel’s mesh The file records the points’ positions and which points form each face. The second and third pictures show the same panel . The dots and lines reveal how its shape is represented; they are not extra physical pieces. Several meshes can belong to one link. Here, the drawer’s shape files describe what to draw, while its joint tells the whole drawer how to slide.

title: Joint, link, and visual origins
text: 3.2.5 Joint, link, and visual origins Now place the drawer in the cabinet. The body is the parent link and the drawer is the child link . URDF needs to know where the drawer starts and where to draw its shapes. Body Drawer One side panel O The body’s starting point We measure positions on the cabinet from here. In this model, the points in the drawer’s shape files were also measured from O. J The drawer’s starting point The drawer uses J as its own zero point. At this closed position, J is also the joint’s starting point. The shape files still use O as their zero. The visual origin tells URDF where that saved zero is relative to J. O → J Joint origin Start at the body’s origin O. Where is the drawer’s starting point J? The joint origin gives that offset. J → O Visual origin, in this model Now start at J. Where is the mesh file’s old zero point O? The visual origin gives the offset back, so the panel is placed correctly around the drawer. The cabinet uses O as its zero point; the drawer uses J as its zero point. In this closed pose, the two frames point the same way. The offsets O → J and J → O are therefore equal and opposite: their coordinates add to zero.

title: 3.3 Reading a URDF file
text: 3.3 Reading a URDF file A URDF file tells us what the parts are, what they look like, and how they connect. Let’s read one using the cabinet we already know.

title: One file, parts and connections
text: 3.3.1 One file, parts and connections The whole model sits inside <robot> . Inside it, <link> describes a part, and <joint> connects two parts. The word “robot” is simply the format’s name for the whole model; this one is a cabinet. A pair such as <link> … </link> marks the beginning and end of a block. A tag ending in /> is complete on its own. The file’s outline <robot name="cabinet"> <link name="base" /> <link name="link_2"> … </link> <link name="link_0"> … </link> <link name="link_1"> … </link> <joint name="joint_2" type="fixed"> … </joint> <joint name="joint_0" type="prismatic"> … </joint> <joint name="joint_1" type="revolute"> … </joint> </robot> This outline leaves out the details. Each … stands for lines inside that block. The connections it describes base Reference link · no shape joint_2 · fixed ↓ Cabinet body link_2 joint_0 · slides ↓ Drawer link_0 joint_1 · rotates ↓ Door link_1 The file lists the parts; the joints make the tree. The drawer’s link is not written inside the body’s link. A joint connects them by naming one as its parent and the other as its child . Names such as link_0 are identifiers. Here they mean “drawer”; another model could use drawer directly. What matters is using the same name when referring to that part.

title: Link: shapes that move together
text: 3.3.2 Link: shapes that move together The drawer’s sides, bottom, front, and handle all move together, so they belong to one link . A link can contain several <visual> blocks, each describing a shape to draw. ⤢ These five pieces form the drawer front. They move together as part of one drawer , so they share one sliding joint. Reading one visual block This excerpt describes the red top strip in the picture. Positions are rounded here to make the code easier to read. <link name="link_0"> <visual name="drawer_front-14"> <origin xyz="0.0142 -0.5376 -0.4921" /> <geometry> <mesh filename="textured_objs/original-34.obj" /> </geometry> </visual> <!-- The other drawer shapes go here too. --> </link> link The whole drawer. All shapes inside this link follow the drawer’s motion. visual One visible shape belonging to that drawer. origin Places this shape relative to the drawer’s own zero point. geometry mesh Describes the shape. Here, mesh tells the viewer which 3D shape file to open. <geometry> can also contain a simple <box> , <cylinder> , or <sphere> . A separate mesh file is not required for every shape. This drawer has 14 visual blocks but only one sliding joint . More shape files do not mean more degrees of freedom.

title: Joint: let the drawer slide
text: 3.3.3 Joint: let the drawer slide A <joint> answers a different question: how can this part move relative to the part it is attached to? Here the body is the parent, and the drawer is the child. <joint name="joint_0" type="prismatic"> <parent link="link_2" /> <child link="link_0" /> <origin xyz="-0.0142 0.5376 0.4921" /> <axis xyz="0 0 1" /> <limit lower="0" upper="0.76" /> </joint> type Prismatic means sliding. The drawer moves along a straight line. parent child Connect the body ( link_2 ) to the drawer ( link_0 ). origin Locates the joint’s starting frame relative to the body. The red dot marks the drawer’s starting point when closed, called J in the previous chapter. axis 0 0 1 means the joint’s positive Z direction. For this drawer, that points outward. limit The allowed travel is 0 to 0.76 meters : from closed to 76 cm open. ⤢ The dashed outline marks the closed drawer. Here, q = 76 cm : the blue drawer is fully open. One degree of freedom, one number The drawer’s sliding joint has one degree of freedom : it lets the drawer move in and out. One number is enough to describe its position. We call that number q , the distance the drawer has opened. q = 0 cm: the drawer is closed. q = 30 cm: it is partly open. q = 76 cm: it is fully open in this model. The limit sets the allowed range, 0–76 cm . The value of q tells us where the drawer is right now within that range.

title: Joint: let the door rotate
text: 3.3.4 Joint: let the door rotate The door uses the same structure, with a different motion type. Revolute means a hinge with a limited angle. <joint name="joint_1" type="revolute"> <parent link="link_2" /> <child link="link_1" /> <origin xyz="-0.3577 -0.5906 0.4916" /> <axis xyz="0 -1 0" /> <limit lower="0" upper="1.5708" /> </joint> The origin places the joint’s starting point at the hinge. The axis gives the direction of the hinge line through that point. Here 0 -1 0 points downward in the joint’s frame. ⤢ The door turns around the purple hinge line . The dashed outline shows it closed. Here, q = 90° : the solid door is fully open. Rotating joints use radians in the file: 1.5708 radians is approximately 90° . So this door is allowed to open from 0° to 90°. The picture shows it at that upper limit. This hinge also has one degree of freedom . For the door, q is the opening angle ; for the drawer, q is the opening distance. A wheel that can keep turning without an angular stop would use type="continuous" instead. It has a rotation axis but no lower or upper position limit.

title: How a part looks and behaves
text: 3.3.5 How a part looks and behaves A link can describe three things about a part, such as this cabinet body: visual The shape you see. Draws the cabinet body and the shelf inside it. collision The shape used to check contact. For example, it tells the simulator whether a box touches the shelf. inertial How heavy the part is and how its mass is spread out. Helps calculate how it responds to pushes and turns. ⤢ This shelf uses the same 3D shape for visual and collision : one shape for drawing it and checking contact. This cabinet file includes visual and collision data. It has no inertial blocks, so it does not specify how heavy the parts are.

title: Why is there an extra base link?
text: 3.3.6 Why is there an extra base link? Our cabinet has three visible parts, yet the file has four links. The extra one is base , an invisible reference for the whole cabinet . The fixed joint joint_2 places the cabinet body relative to that reference. <link name="base" /> <joint name="joint_2" type="fixed"> <parent link="base" /> <child link="link_2" /> <origin xyz="0 0 0" rpy="1.5708 0 -1.5708" /> </joint> A fixed joint can set an orientation The rpy numbers store a rotation. In this example, that rotation turns the cabinet body into the intended orientation. Fixed means the body keeps that orientation relative to the base. There is no extra movement to control. ⤢ Both the middle and right examples remove the base and fixed joint. The right example takes one extra step: it rotates the whole cabinet in the scene to restore the original orientation. These pictures show starting poses, before any physics simulation. Can we leave out the base and fixed joint? Yes, with two steps: remove both elements so the cabinet body becomes the root, then apply the original fixed joint’s rotation to the whole cabinet when placing it in the scene. The drawer and door can then move exactly as before. Keeping base and joint_2 stores the rotation inside the URDF. Removing both moves that responsibility to how we place the model in the scene. What if we remove only the fixed joint? The base link would be left disconnected from the cabinet. We would have two separate roots: base and the cabinet body. A URDF needs one connected tree, so a standard URDF loader rejects this arrangement. None of the three pictures shows this disconnected case. The fixed joint adds zero degrees of freedom . With the cabinet held still, the drawer and door still provide two independent movements: one slide and one rotation. Cabinet URDF ↗ URDF reference ↗

title: 3.4 What happens when we change the URDF?
text: 3.4 What happens when we change the URDF? Use the same cabinet to see what changes when we edit its joints and shapes.

title: Change the drawer’s direction
text: 3.4.1 Change the drawer’s direction The drawer’s axis tells it which way to slide. Here we change only that direction. The starting point and the 0–76 cm travel range stay the same. The +X, +Y, and +Z arrows show the joint’s reference directions at its closed pose. In this cabinet, +X points sideways, +Y points up, and +Z points out of the front . These are the joint’s local axes; the scene can use a different up axis. The purple arrow shows the chosen sliding direction. Out of the cabinet ⤢ <axis xyz=" 0 0 1 " /> 0 0 1 means +Z: increasing q pulls the drawer outward. Into the cabinet ⤢ <axis xyz=" 0 0 -1 " /> 0 0 −1 means −Z: the purple arrow points opposite +Z. Keeping the same positive range now sends the drawer inward. Along a diagonal ⤢ The purple arrow combines +X and +Y : sideways and upward together. <axis xyz=" 0.707107 0.707107 0 " /> Read xyz in order: X, then Y, then Z . The two equal positive numbers mean “move sideways along +X and upward along +Y by equal amounts.” The final 0 means no movement along Z. For example, after sliding 10 cm along the purple arrow, the drawer has moved about 7.1 cm sideways and 7.1 cm upward . This is still one degree of freedom. The drawer follows one straight line. It cannot choose its upward and sideways movements separately. One number, q , tells us how far it has moved along that line. The cabinet is transparent so you can see the path. These animations follow the motion written in the file; they do not stop parts at collisions.

title: Turn a hinged door into a sliding door
text: 3.4.2 Turn a hinged door into a sliding door For a hinge, axis gives the line the door rotates around . For a slide, it gives the direction the door moves along . Changing revolute to prismatic also changes the limit from an angle to a distance. Original hinged door ⤢ type="revolute" <axis xyz="0 -1 0" /> <limit lower="0" upper="1.5708" /> 0 −1 0 points along −Y , down the vertical hinge. The door turns around that line. 1.5708 radians is about 90°. Change only the type ⤢ type=" prismatic " <axis xyz="0 -1 0" /> <limit lower="0" upper="1.5708" /> The same −Y axis now means slide downward . The same upper limit now means 1.5708 meters . This movement is set by the joint, not by gravity. Make it slide sideways ⤢ 1 0 0 means +X: the door slides sideways across the front of the cabinet. type=" prismatic " <axis xyz=" 1 0 0 " /> <limit lower="0" upper=" 0.7 " /> We change three things together: Type: slide instead of rotate. Axis: move sideways instead of downward. Limit: travel 70 cm. The door still has one DOF . Its q now measures distance instead of angle.

title: Remove the drawer
text: 3.4.3 Remove the drawer To remove this drawer, delete both its link and the joint connecting it to the cabinet . With the drawer ⤢ Cabinet body ├── Drawer · joint_0 └── Door · joint_1 Two movable parts: the drawer and the door. Without the drawer ⤢ Cabinet body └── Door · joint_1 The door still works. The drawer opening remains because it is part of the cabinet body. In this file, remove the entire <link name="link_0"> block and the entire <joint name="joint_0"> block. Deleting only the link would leave a joint pointing to a drawer that no longer exists. Deleting only the joint would leave the drawer disconnected. This drawer has no parts attached beneath it in the tree, so the other connections can stay as they are.

title: Swap the shapes, keep the joints
text: 3.4.4 Swap the shapes, keep the joints What if the drawer used the door’s joint, and the door used the drawer’s joint? Original shapes ⤢ The blue drawer slides. The gold door swings. Shapes swapped ⤢ The blue drawer shape swings. The gold door panel slides. The joint sets the movement, whatever shape we attach to it. Calling a link “drawer” or giving it a drawer shape does not automatically make it slide. Link and joint Original shape New shape link_0 · sliding joint Drawer Door panel link_1 · hinge joint Door panel Drawer For this example, we exchange the two links’ visual and collision blocks. We also adjust their placement offsets so both shapes still start in the same closed positions. The joints keep their original locations, directions, and limits. The result is an unusual cabinet, but it makes the roles clear: the shapes describe the parts; the joints describe their movement. Cabinet URDF ↗ URDF reference ↗

title: 3.5 From animation to simulation
text: 3.5 From animation to simulation A box moves down toward a table. We can create that movement in two different ways.

title: Two ways to move a box
text: 3.5.1 Two ways to move a box We choose the positions “Start here. Move down. Stop here.” The box follows the positions we chose. We do not calculate gravity or contact for this animation. We calculate the motion “Put the box here, then let go.” The simulator calculates the movement. Gravity makes the box fall; contact with the table stops it. Table height 40 cm Lower Higher Gravity on Both boxes reach the table. Raise the table to see the difference. Both examples repeat from the same starting position. The box on the right starts at rest, with no air resistance or bounce. The interactive comparison needs JavaScript. The explanations below describe what each change would do.

title: Change the scene
text: 3.5.2 Change the scene Raise the table On the left, the box keeps following its saved path. It passes through the raised tabletop because we have not changed its positions or added a contact rule. On the right, the box meets the higher table sooner and rests on its surface. The simulator calculates a new result from the changed scene. Turn gravity off On the left, the saved movement continues. On the right, the box stays where we release it. It starts with no speed, and there is now no force pulling it down. We could edit the left animation to match either result. With the simulation, we change the scene or its physical settings and calculate the movement again.

title: Back to the drawer
text: 3.5.3 Back to the drawer The cabinet GIFs in the previous chapter work like the box on the left. We choose the drawer’s opening distance, q , at each moment: closed, a little open, farther open, and back again. To simulate a pull, we give the drawer mass, describe friction, and apply a pulling force. Its joint still restricts it to sliding. The simulator calculates how fast it moves and how its opening distance changes. The examples below do this. Our current GIF We choose q → draw the drawer there. Physics simulation We apply a pull → calculate the movement → get q. A simulation can also produce an animation. Either result can be saved as a GIF or video. The difference is how the positions were produced. A falling-box example in MuJoCo ↗

title: Pull the drawer
text: 3.5.4 Pull the drawer A force is a push or a pull. We measure it in newtons, written N . A 3 N pull is three times as strong as a 1 N pull. It does not tell us how many centimeters the drawer will open. Here we pull each drawer for half a second , then let go. Both start closed and still. Both have a mass of 2 kg, and we leave out friction for this first comparison. ⤢ The stronger pull makes the same drawer gain speed faster. After the same amount of time, it has opened farther. The green arrow shows the pull; the blue measurement shows q. We chose the force, not the ending position. The opening distances come from calculating the motion and drawing each resulting position. These are side-view teaching examples with chosen values, not measurements of the earlier cabinet. The cabinet stays fixed, and its rails keep the drawer moving horizontally. Only forces along the slide are shown. The GIFs play slowly and hold their last frame before replaying.

title: Same pull, different mass
text: 3.5.5 Same pull, different mass Now keep the pull the same: 3 N for half a second . Change only the moving mass, from 2 kg to 4 kg . Think of adding items to the drawer. Friction is still left out so we can see the effect of mass by itself. ⤢ The heavier drawer gains speed more slowly under the same pull. It opens less during this example. This is why the simulator needs mass. Two drawers can look identical and have the same sliding joint, yet respond differently to the same pull.

title: Friction can resist the pull
text: 3.5.6 Friction can resist the pull Have you pulled a drawer gently and found that it would not budge? Friction can balance a weak pull and keep the drawer still. Once the drawer slides, friction acts against that sliding movement. Both drawers below have a mass of 2 kg and receive the same 3 N pull . Only the friction in their rails changes. ⤢ Green points in the pulling direction. Orange shows friction pushing against the pull or the sliding movement. The easy-sliding drawer starts moving, with 0.8 N of friction opposing the 3 N pull. The stiff rails can resist a pull of up to 4 N before sliding starts . With our 3 N pull, their friction only needs to provide 3 N in the opposite direction. The forces balance, so that drawer stays still. Applying a force does not guarantee movement. We have to account for the other forces too.

title: What happens after letting go?
text: 3.5.7 What happens after letting go? Removing the pull does not instantly stop a moving drawer. In this example, both drawers are already moving outward at 40 cm per second . They are both 10 cm open when we let go. ⤢ Without friction or another opposing force, the drawer keeps its speed. With friction, it slows down and stops. Neither drawer reaches its 76 cm travel limit in this clip. The drawer does not automatically close when we let go. That would need something else, such as a spring or a closing force. Here, each replay simply restarts the example. The sliding joint still has one degree of freedom : q tells us the opening distance. The force changes how q develops over time; it does not add another degree of freedom. Force and mass ↗ Friction ↗ Motion after release ↗
